Considering the contemporary trends toward increased commodification, virtualization, and homogenization of computing and network resources I think we will see the development of a Semantic Web building on a kind of blockchain-based distributed computing environment where the network becomes both a communications network and a 'blind' processing environment for software that exists independently of location and hardware. A global cloud computing environment. In effect, this is how we might realize the futurist concept of 'computronium'--a kind of generic computational matter slowly subsuming the built habitat.

Here's another way to picture this. We know networking is becoming more ubiquitous in the infrastructure of the built habitat. And the trends in personal computing are increasingly toward cloud computing use. So the mainstream personal computer user is increasingly relying on things like phones and tablets linked by WiFi. The trend in design for these devices is toward increasing minimalism. Most people want ease of use, take-it-for-granted reliability, and convenience over high performance yet bulky and quirky hardware--hence the slow decline in desktop PCs. We're heading for an era where phones, tablets, laptops, tabletop, and wall screens are going to be really minimalist things, maybe 4mm thick. (like a clip-board) And that favors off-loading processing and data storage to the cloud to allow for progressive front-end hardware minimalism.

The chief trend in server evolution is 'virtualization'. System platforms that conceal or hide the specifics of hardware architectures to make server functions more generic--to reduce their characteristics to just commodity performance factors. Because market share in that realm of computing is very much driven by interoperability. It's got to be generic. Any distinct, proprietary, feature of a system is a management bottleneck. A hassle. Storage and processing are now generic commodities. And another reason for this virtualization is security. You now can't trust the people who make your hardware--especially if they're in regressive nations like China and the United States. So virtualization is leading to increasingly 'blind' and decentralized processing where what's actually being stored and processed is encrypted and the systems just push data around without being able to 'see' what it is. And this has led to the concept of blockchain-based cloud computing. Systems where a blockchain is setup P2P among a community of users as a blind encrypted cloud distributed redundantly across all the bits of hardware the community puts into it. Imagine if Bitcoin was your hard drive and then your computer. That's where we're heading. First that's going to be specialized storage. Then it's going to be hosting services, like encrypted mail, other communications, semantic webs, services like OpenBazaar. Then it's going to be storage and processing in general. A big generic cloud computer that can never be turned off. And it's going to be more and more distributed geographically, the hardware for it will get more and more generic, and it will sink further and further into the infrastructure.

So the future of the Internet and personal computing looks like a bunch PADs--front-end devices--in many sizes and forms supported on an always-on indestructible cloud computing network composed of blind generic storage, processing, and routing modules spread all over the place. And if you need more performance locally, for things like science/engineering computing or high-performance gaming, you'll put more of those modules in your house/building so they are more immediate to your PADs, or you might have specialized PADs, but they will still run blind. All the software and data will be in the encrypted global cloud and programs will function as--more-or-less--indestructible entities running on the cloud independent of location. And that cloud node hardware will just get smaller, denser, more generic, more distributed until it becomes that computronium--that generic universal processing matter all over the built habitat.
